messages.author: b8863e2cc3f8818f
messages.subject: Hierarchical model in 8schools data: Exceptions and divergent transitions
parts:
Dear all,

I am using a somewhat different parametrization of a Bayesian hierarchical model for the schools data (compared to the Rstan tutorial) and get exceptions and warnings about divergent transitions, even after adjusting adapt_delta to 0.99 (see Model, Command, Output below). How should I interpret this and deal with it?

Thanks in advance, Wilmar

## Model
data {  int<lower=0> J;
        real y[J];
        real<lower=0> sigma[J];
        real mu0;
        real<lower=0> tauScale;
      }

parameters {
        real theta[J];
        real mu;
        real<lower=0> tau;
}

model {
        mu ~ normal(mu0, 10000);        // standard deviation is 10^4
        tau ~ cauchy(0, tauScale);      // scale
        theta ~ normal(mu, tau);
        y ~ normal(theta, sigma);
}

## Command
fit <- stan(file = file.path, data = schools_dat,
            iter = 1000, chains = 1, control=list(adapt_delta=0.80))

You interpret it as the centered parameterization being a poor choice and you
deal with it by switching to a non-centered parameterization, as per the RStan
tutorial.  When you have sparse data it’s almost impossible to fit a centered
parametrized model.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Hierarchical model in 8schools data: Exceptions and divergent transitions
parts:
On Thursday, November 26, 2015 at 11:57:46 AM UTC-5, Wilmar Igl wrote:
I am using a somewhat different parametrization of a Bayesian hierarchical model for the schools data (compared to the Rstan tutorial) and get exceptions and warnings about divergent transitions, even after adjusting adapt_delta to 0.99 (see Model, Command, Output below). How should I interpret this and deal with it?

I would interpret this as saying the parameterization you are using is less amenable to HMC as the one in the RStan tutorial. The parameterization of the 8 schools model is not best for all hierarchical models, but it often is. You could increase adapt_delta more, but not all problems with divergent transitions can be overcome with a higher target acceptance probability. You need to look at the pairs() plot like the warning suggests to see where the numerical problems are occurring. Divergent transitions near the mode (particularly that have a high probability of being accepted and plotted in the upper triangle) can usually be squashed with a sufficiently high adapt_delta, while divergent transitions in the tail (particularly that have a low probability of being accepted and plotted in the lower triangle) often mean that you should try to reparameterize the model, which is likely in your case.

Ben

P.S. You should also update your version of rstan.

messages.subject: Re: Hierarchical model in 8schools data: Exceptions and divergent transitions
parts:
Dear Bob,

after running the schools data with the non-centered hierarchical model (as suggested)  the efficiency in terms of effective sample size of iterations increased by a factor 2 to 3. The results of the centered and non-centered models were very similar. I checked the convergence behaviour with traceplots visually and using Rhat values  (all relevant parameters < 1.02), which showed good mixing of four chains of both approaches. However, also the non-centered model gave a low number (< 20) of divergent transitions when running with adept_delta of 0.8.

What is the best way to reduce divergent transitions? At the moment it seems using a non-centered model and setting adept_delta to 0.99 is the preferred solution.

What do you (or others) think?

Best, Wilmar

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical model in 8schools data: Exceptions and divergent transitions
parts:
If you can get them to converge, they should definitely both give you
the same posterior (to within MCMC std error, of course).

If the divergences are happening during warmup, you also
want to set a stepsize (name of R control parameter) lower than the default.
I have a feeling we're going to be changing our default at some point to make
it lower.

You might also be able to control divergence with tighter priors.

- Bob
